title: Ten Percent Off Doesn't Cost You Ten Percent of Profit. It Costs More.
linkedin:
Black Friday is four weeks out. Most discount codes being set across the East Coast right now are built on a feeling, not a number.

Here's the calculation that rarely gets done before the sale goes live: a discount comes straight off your margin, not off the full sale price. Take a business running a 30 percent gross margin that discounts a line by 10 percent for Black Friday. That 10 percent is a third of the profit dollar on every unit sold at that price.

To make the same total gross profit as if the sale never happened, that business needs to sell roughly 50 percent more units of that line across the promotion. Not the modest lift most owners picture when they picture a sale "bringing people in".

Push the discount to 20 percent on that same margin and the required lift roughly doubles. Shrink the starting margin to 15 percent and a 10 percent discount needs close to triple the volume just to break even.

The pattern we see across owner-led businesses heading into the Christmas trading peak is that the discount depth gets chosen on instinct, and the required volume lift only gets calculated in January, against a margin result that does not match the revenue everyone was celebrating in December.

The fix takes minutes, not a major project. Pull last year's sales by product line, work out the actual margin on each, then divide the discount by the gap between margin and discount. That single number is your break-even volume lift, and it is worth knowing before the code goes live.

Black Friday is four weeks away and Christmas trading sits right behind it, which means most business owners across Brisbane, Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria are finalising discount codes and sale signage for the final quarter right now. Before locking in a discount percentage, it is worth doing one quick calculation.

A discount comes straight off your profit margin, not off the full sale price. A business running a 30 percent margin that discounts a line by 10 percent needs to sell roughly 50 percent more units of that line just to make the same total profit it would have made without running the sale at all. As the starting margin gets thinner, that required volume lift climbs even faster, which is exactly the position a lot of hospitality, retail and trade businesses are in heading into their busiest weeks of the year.

The good news is the calculation itself takes minutes. Pull last year's sales by product or service line, work out the real margin on each, and divide the discount percentage by the gap between the margin and the discount. That gives a break-even volume figure worth knowing before the sale goes live, not after the quarter closes.
